content: Podoplanin (PDPN) is a protein in humans encoded by the PDPN gene. It is a mucin-type protein with a molecular mass ranging from 36 to 43 kDa. This protein is relatively conserved across species, with homologues identified in humans, mice, rats, dogs, and hamsters. The PDPN gene encodes a type-I, integral membrane glycoprotein that is heavily O-glycosylated and exhibits diverse distribution across human tissues. Its physiological function is thought to be related to its mucin-like properties. In other species, the homologous protein has been described as a differentiation antigen and a receptor for influenza viruses. While the precise function of podoplanin remains undetermined, it has been proposed as a marker of lung injury. Alternative splicing of the PDPN gene results in transcript variants encoding different isoforms. Podoplanin has been identified as playing roles in various cell types, including lung alveolar cells, kidney podocytes, and lymphatic endothelial cells. More recently, it has also been detected in neural tissues in both mouse and human samples. In lymphatic endothelial cells, experimental evidence suggests that podoplanin is involved in the proper formation of connections between the cardiovascular and lymphatic systems. In mice, disruptions in this process have been associated with fatty liver disease. Although its exact function in many tissues remains unclear, podoplanin is detectable via immunofluorescent staining and has been shown to co-localize with nestin, a type VI intermediate filament protein predominantly expressed in neural tissues. The only known physiological interaction partner of podoplanin is CLEC-2, a C-type lectin expressed on platelets and hematopoietic cells. Together, podoplanin and CLEC-2 are essential for the proper formation of blood and lymphatic connections during embryonic development. From a clinical perspective, PDPN has been extensively studied in the context of cancer. It serves as a specific marker for lymphatic vessels, and since levels of lymphangiogenesis are correlated with poor prognosis in cancer patients, PDPN can be used as a diagnostic marker. It is frequently upregulated in certain cancers, including various squamous cell carcinomas, malignant mesothelioma, and brain tumors. Additionally, cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) in the tumor stroma can upregulate PDPN, which has been linked to poor prognosis. In squamous cell carcinomas, PDPN is believed to play a critical role in cancer cell invasiveness by regulating invadopodia, thereby facilitating efficient degradation of the extracellular matrix (ECM).
